newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada seeks to expel suspected Nazi war criminal.
newsitem.headline: Canada seeks to expel suspected Nazi war criminal.

text.p: Canada is seeking to expel an 83-year-old Latvian, allegedly involved in grisly war crimes against Jews, Communists and Red Army personnel during World War Two, an immigration hearing was told on Wednesday.
Konrad Kalejs, who is suffering from cancer, listened attentively at the hearing as a Canadian goverment lawyer detailed his alleged involvement with Latvian Nazi death squads.
The government is in the final stages of a bid to expel Kalejs from the country.

Kalejs, who also has a heart condition and is heavily medicated, waved dismissively as the government sought to discredit his claim that he was a university student at the time and not a leader of special death squads against "destructive elements."
"The testimony is incredible and totally unbelievable," immigration lawyer Donald MacIntosh told the hearing that gone on sporadically since last February.
MacIntosh said Kalejs was in university but had long absences in the early 1940s due to his position as first lieutenant with the Arajs Kommando.
MacIntosh said the group murdered and kidnapped people to rid the region of so-called destructive elements. "They hunted down the Communists, the Red Army and Jews," the lawyer said.
He described as incredible Kalejs' claim that he was not present when the Arajs Kommando participated in the massacre of Jews in a Latvian forest in December 1941.
Canadian officials said Kalejs lived in Australia after the war and then moved to the United States where he was deported after a long case in 1994.
Kalejs was allowed only temporary entry to Canada after he was stopped at the airport by Immigration officials in 1995. But he remained in the country.
The case comes amid concern that Canada has become a haven for Nazi war criminals.
The Jerusalem Post reported in November that an American investigator uncovered 157 alleged Nazi criminals, many of them from Latvia and Lithuania, believed to be living comfortably in Canada.

Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock has promised to investigate the new charges, but the report was greeted with resigned dismay by Canadian Jewish groups who believe Ottawa has not worked hard enough to prosecute former Nazis.
The goverment expects to finish its summary in the Kalejs case this week, while counsel for Kalejs will have their turn beginning next Monday.
"The case has gone pretty well," said Kalejs's lawyer, Win Thompson, after the proceedings. "There have been no surprises."
